question: How many separate bones are typically found in a healthy adult human body?
explanation: An adult human skeleton typically consists of 206 distinct bones after various smaller bones fuse together during childhood development. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T4#GNS121_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why do we call bones a living organ system instead of just dry structures?

options.A: It changes its shape solely due to external pressure from tight clothing
options.B: It is made entirely of soft muscle tissue that continuously moves on its own
options.C: It contains active cells, blood vessels, and nerves that respond to the body's needs
options.D: It grows larger only by absorbing water from the surrounding skin tissues

explanation: You got this! Bones aren't just dead sticks; they are packed with blood and nerves so they can repair themselves and react to stress.

question: Which bone cells are responsible for breaking down or resorbing bone tissue?
explanation: Think of OsteoCLASTS as 'clearing' out bone to help reshape it and release calcium when your body needs it. You're learning fast!

question: What do collagen fibers mainly give to our bones?
explanation: Collagen is like the tough rubber bands inside bone—it gives flexibility so they bend slightly instead of shattering like glass.

question: What is the tiny, functional building block of compact bone called?
explanation: An osteon is just the neat, cylinder-shaped repeating unit that makes up hard compact bone. Brilliant work!

question: A patient falls and cracks the hard outer layer of their thigh bone (femur). Which bone tissue is affected?
explanation: Compact bone forms that tough, dense outer shield of long bones. You'll see this often in orthopaedic wards!

question: Which bone shape category does the patella ( kneecap) belong to?
explanation: Sesamoid bones like the patella develop inside tendons to protect them from excessive wear and tear. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T4#GNS121_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is the main job of flat bones in the body?

options.A: Absorbing high impact forces in tight spaces like the wrist
options.B: Acting as long levers to propel the body forward during running
options.C: Guiding tendons smoothly across major joints without friction
options.D: Protecting internal organs and providing broad muscle attachment sites

explanation: Flat bones (like your skull and sternum) act like helmets and shields for vital organs while giving muscles a wide place to anchor.

question: Which of these is a part of the axial skeleton?
explanation: The axial skeleton runs right down the middle—think skull, spine, and chest cage. You're doing great!

question: What is the main job of the appendicular skeleton?

options.A: Maintaining the central structural axis for upright balance
options.B: Protecting the delicate structures of the central nervous system
options.C: Facilitating body movement and interacting with the environment
options.D: Housing the bone marrow that produces white blood cells

explanation: The appendicular skeleton includes your arms, legs, and shoulders—built for moving around and grabbing things!

question: What is the main job of red bone marrow?

options.D: Releasing calcium ions directly into bone

explanation: Red marrow is our body's busy factory for making red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Excellent!

question: Why is bone considered an important storage bank for the whole body?

options.A: It burns stored fat tissue to maintain a stable body temperature
options.B: It produces hormones that regulate the speed of digestion
options.C: It filters waste products directly out of the circulating blood supply
options.D: It stores large amounts of essential minerals like calcium and phosphorus

explanation: Bones hold onto key minerals and release them into the blood whenever your nerves and muscles need them. Perfect!

question: Which part of a child's bone allows it to grow longer as they get older?
explanation: The epiphyseal plate is also called the growth plate. Once adulthood is reached, it closes up! You're mastering this.

question: How do bones react when you do regular physical exercise and put mechanical stress on them?

options.A: They become fragile and brittle because osteoclasts destroy the matrix
options.B: They stop all cellular remodeling to conserve mineral reserves
options.C: They become thicker and stronger through increased osteoblast activity
options.D: They convert entirely from compact bone into spongy bone tissue

explanation: Use them and strengthen them! Exercise signals bone-building osteoblasts to lay down more material, making bones tough.

question: What is the main worry with osteoporosis that nurses must look out for?

options.A: Severe bacterial inflammation spreading throughout the bone marrow
options.B: Excessive mineral deposition causing bones to become overly rigid
options.C: Abnormal hardening of the joints preventing any physical movement
options.D: Decreased bone mass and density leading to a high risk of fractures

explanation: Osteoporosis makes bones porous and fragile, meaning even a small bump can lead to a painful fracture. Great clinical insight!

question: As a nurse, what is your most important duty when caring for an elderly patient with severe osteoporosis?

options.A: Applying continuous heavy traction to strengthen weak leg bones
options.B: Restricting dietary calcium intake to prevent mineral crystal buildup
options.C: Implementing strict fall prevention protocols in the environment
options.D: Encouraging complete bed rest to prevent accidental bone trauma

explanation: Prevention is key! Keeping the environment safe from slips and trips protects fragile bones from breaking. Excellent nursing care!
